needs.title: Following and stopping distance

source_cards.front: Which of these affects your stopping distance?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance depends on how long it takes you to notice danger, the type and condition of the road, your tire tread and your brakes.

source_cards.front: What following distance does the MVA recommend in ideal conditions?
source_cards.back: Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes, and the MVA recommends at least three to four seconds of following distance in ideal conditions.

source_cards.front: What following distance should you keep behind buses and delivery vans?
source_cards.back: Behind vehicles that stop often, such as buses and delivery vans, increase your following distance to four or five seconds, or more if needed.

source_cards.front: How is following distance different from stopping distance?
source_cards.back: Following distance is measured in seconds against a fixed reference point, whereas stopping distance depends on reaction time, road surface, tire tread and brakes.

needs.title: Intersections and right-of-way

source_cards.front: What does yielding the right-of-way mean?
source_cards.back: Yielding the right-of-way means letting another vehicle, bicyclist or pedestrian go first, and you should never assume you automatically have the right to go first.

source_cards.front: At a four-way stop, whom must you always yield to?
source_cards.back: At a four-way intersection with stop signs, yield to the driver on your right, and always yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers still in the intersection.

source_cards.front: Who goes first at an intersection when drivers arrive at different times?
source_cards.back: First to arrive goes first at an intersection, and only when two drivers arrive together does the driver on the right get the right-of-way.

needs.title: Passing and no-passing situations

source_cards.front: When may you drive left of the center of the road?
source_cards.back: Keep right of the center of the road unless you are passing a vehicle going your way, a sign or signal permits it, or an obstruction makes moving over necessary.

source_cards.front: When may you return to your lane after passing?
source_cards.back: Before passing, judge the time and space needed, signal, pass at a safe distance, and return to your lane only when both headlights of the passed vehicle show in your rear-view mirror.

source_cards.front: On which side should you normally pass?
source_cards.back: Pass on the left as a rule; passing on the right is allowed only when safe and on the road, when the other vehicle is turning left or you are on an unobstructed road or one-way road with two or more lanes in your direction.

source_cards.front: Which center line marking bans passing when it is on your side?
source_cards.back: Do not pass in a no-passing zone, where the solid yellow center line is on your side, at double solid yellow lines, or when passing would interfere with other vehicles.

source_cards.front: Where do double solid yellow lines ban passing?
source_cards.back: A single solid yellow center line bans passing when it is on your side of the road, while double solid yellow lines ban passing wherever they appear.

needs.title: Turning paths and lanes

source_cards.front: When turning left, whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: When turning left, yield to drivers in the opposing lane, meaning traffic coming from the opposite direction.

source_cards.front: Which signal do you use for a U-turn?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is signaled with the left turn signal and ends in the outside, right-hand lane of the opposite direction, not the lane nearest the center.

source_cards.front: On which side should you normally pass?
source_cards.back: Pass on the left as a rule; passing on the right is allowed only when safe and on the road, when the other vehicle is turning left or you are on an unobstructed road or one-way road with two or more lanes in your direction.

source_cards.front: Is passing on the right ever allowed on the shoulder?
source_cards.back: Passing on the right is an exception allowed only when it is safe, you stay on the road, and the other vehicle is turning left or you are on an unobstructed road with two or more lanes your way; it is never allowed on the shoulder.

needs.title: Crosswalks and stop positions

source_cards.front: Where do you stop at a signal that is not working when there is no stop line?
source_cards.back: When a traffic signal is not working, stop at the clearly marked stop line, which is a wide white line painted across the road; with no stop line, stop before the crosswalk; with neither, stop before entering the intersection.

source_cards.front: How long do you stay stopped at a dark signal compared with a steady red?
source_cards.back: A dark, non-working signal and a steady red both require a stop at the stop line, crosswalk or intersection edge, but at a dark signal you stay stopped only until it is safe to enter and continue through.

source_cards.front: What does a steady red signal require?
source_cards.back: At a steady red signal, stop completely at the stop line, or before the crosswalk and intersection if there is none, and stay stopped while the light is red.

source_cards.front: What does a steady red arrow mean for the direction it points?
source_cards.back: A steady red arrow means that if you want to go the way it points, you stop completely before the stop line, crosswalk or intersection and stay stopped while the arrow is red.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a flashing red signal?
source_cards.back: At a flashing red signal, stop completely at the stop line, or before the crosswalk and intersection, yield to all traffic and pedestrians, and go when the way is clear.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing red arrow allow?
source_cards.back: A flashing red arrow means stop completely before the stop line, crosswalk or intersection, yield to all traffic and pedestrians, then go in the arrow's direction when clear.

source_cards.front: How is a crosswalk signal activated?
source_cards.back: A crosswalk signal halts traffic so pedestrians can cross safely; a pedestrian activates it with a push button on a roadside pole, and it signals drivers to stop before telling pedestrians to cross.

source_cards.front: For drivers at a crosswalk signal, what does solid yellow mean?
source_cards.back: For drivers at a crosswalk signal, flashing yellow means slow down, solid yellow means get ready to stop, solid red means stop, and flashing red means stop and then proceed with caution.

source_cards.back: At a steady red signal, stop completely at the stop line, or before the crosswalk and intersection if there is none, and stay stopped while the light is red.

source_cards.front: After a full stop at a red light, when may you turn left?
source_cards.back: Unless a sign forbids it, after a full stop at a red signal you may turn right, or turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow signal mean?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow signal means the light is changing from green to red, giving you time to stop safely and letting vehicles already in the intersection clear it; if you are too close to stop safely, continue through carefully.

source_cards.front: What must you check first on a steady green signal?
source_cards.back: On a steady green signal, first check that no vehicles are in the intersection, then go straight or turn with caution unless a sign or signal prohibits the turn, yielding to pedestrians and vehicles already there.

source_cards.front: What does a steady red arrow mean for the direction it points?
source_cards.back: A steady red arrow means that if you want to go the way it points, you stop completely before the stop line, crosswalk or intersection and stay stopped while the arrow is red.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow arrow mean?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow arrow means permission to turn that way is ending, so slow down and proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: On a steady green arrow, must you still yield?
source_cards.back: A steady green arrow lets you go with caution in the direction it points, but you must still yield to all pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection.

source_cards.front: How does a steady yellow arrow differ from a flashing yellow light?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow arrow signals that turn permission is ending, while a flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: How does a steady red arrow differ from a flashing red arrow?
source_cards.back: A steady red arrow keeps you stopped while it is red, but a flashing red arrow lets you go in its direction after a full stop once traffic and pedestrians are clear.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a flashing red signal?
source_cards.back: At a flashing red signal, stop completely at the stop line, or before the crosswalk and intersection, yield to all traffic and pedestrians, and go when the way is clear.

source_cards.front: At a railroad crossing with a flashing red signal and no train in sight, what do you do?

source_cards.front: What does a flashing yellow signal mean?
source_cards.back: A flashing yellow signal means you must slow down and proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing red arrow allow?
source_cards.back: A flashing red arrow means stop completely before the stop line, crosswalk or intersection, yield to all traffic and pedestrians, then go in the arrow's direction when clear.

source_cards.front: Over a lane, which signal means never drive in it?
source_cards.back: Never drive in a lane under a red X signal, but you may drive in a lane under a green arrow signal.

source_cards.back: The stop sign, white letters on red, is the only eight-sided sign you will meet on the road.

source_cards.back: Approaching a yield sign, slow down, look left and right, and yield to pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles, then go on only when it is safe.

source_cards.front: What does an orange sign warn of?
source_cards.back: An orange sign warns of a construction or maintenance work area.

source_cards.front: Which signs use white?
source_cards.back: White is used for speed limit signs, keep right signs and some guide signs.

source_cards.front: What does a green sign show?

source_cards.back: Rectangles are regulatory or guide signs: a vertical one usually states an instruction or rule of the road, while a horizontal one usually gives directions or information.

source_cards.front: What does a trapezoid sign mark?
source_cards.back: A trapezoid sign marks recreation and cultural interest areas and National Forest Routes.

source_cards.front: Must you obey regulatory signs?

source_cards.back: White is used for speed limit signs, keep right signs and some guide signs.

source_cards.front: What does a crossbuck sign show?
source_cards.back: A crossbuck sign stands at a highway-rail grade crossing to show exactly where the railroad crossing is.

source_cards.front: How does a round railroad sign differ from a crossbuck?
source_cards.back: A round sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead, while a crossbuck marks the crossing location itself.

source_cards.front: What does a vertical rectangle usually give you?
source_cards.back: Rectangles are regulatory or guide signs: a vertical one usually states an instruction or rule of the road, while a horizontal one usually gives directions or information.

source_cards.front: Must you obey regulatory signs?
source_cards.back: Regulatory signs state traffic laws, and you are required to obey them.

source_cards.front: What does a black-on-white speed limit sign give?
source_cards.back: Rectangular four-sided signs with black lettering on white regulate traffic, and the speed limit sign among them gives the maximum speed for the stretch of road where it stands.

source_cards.front: What do warning signs give road users?
source_cards.back: Warning signs give road users notice of a situation that may not be easy to see in time.

source_cards.front: Which of these warning signs announces a control device ahead?
source_cards.back: Some warning signs announce a control device before you reach it, such as Stop Ahead, Yield Ahead and Signal Ahead.

source_cards.front: Which of these does a road-shape warning sign flag?
source_cards.back: Warning signs also flag the shape of the road, including a sharp right turn, curves, sharp turns, a steep hill and a side road entering ahead.

source_cards.front: Which change does a lane-change warning sign tell you about?
source_cards.back: Other warning signs tell you that lanes or roads are changing: a lane ends and you merge left, two roads merge, the road divides ahead, or a divided road ends ahead.

source_cards.front: Which two signs also appear in the manual's warning sign set?
source_cards.back: The warning sign set in the manual also shows a Slippery When Wet sign and a No Passing Zone sign.

source_cards.front: What do service information and guide signs tell you?
source_cards.back: Service information and guide signs tell you which businesses and services you can reach by taking certain exits.

source_cards.front: Which of these is among the manual's service and guide sign examples?
source_cards.back: Examples of service and guide signs in the manual point to lodging, a hospital, gas, food, an airport, a train station and a park and ride lot.

source_cards.front: What do pavement markings let you do while driving?
source_cards.back: Pavement markings are lines painted on the road that guide and inform you without making you take your eyes off the roadway.

source_cards.front: May you cross a single broken white line to change lanes?
source_cards.back: A single broken white line divides lanes carrying traffic the same way on roads with more than one lane, and you may cross it to change lanes.

source_cards.front: What does a single broken yellow center line allow?
source_cards.back: A single broken yellow line divides traffic moving in opposite directions and allows careful passing from either side; it serves as the center line on two-lane, two-way roads.

source_cards.front: Between same-direction lanes, what does a single solid white line mean?
source_cards.back: A single solid white line marks the right edge of the road and can also divide same-direction lanes where changing lanes is discouraged.

source_cards.front: What do double solid white lines between same-direction lanes mean?
source_cards.back: Double solid white lines side by side divide same-direction lanes where lane changes are not allowed.

source_cards.front: How do broken white, single solid white and double solid white lines differ?
source_cards.back: A broken white line lets you change lanes between same-direction lanes, a single solid white line discourages it, and double solid white lines prohibit it.

source_cards.front: Which edge does a solid white line mark compared with a solid yellow line?
source_cards.back: A solid white line marks the right edge of a road, but a solid yellow line marks the left edge of divided highways, one-way roads and ramps.

source_cards.front: How does a broken yellow center line differ from double solid yellow lines?
source_cards.back: A single broken yellow center line allows careful passing from both sides, while double solid yellow lines forbid passing from both sides.

source_cards.front: What does a single solid yellow line mark on divided highways, one-way roads and ramps?
source_cards.back: A single solid yellow line marks the left edge of divided highways, one-way roads and ramps.

source_cards.front: What else may double solid white lines separate?
source_cards.back: Double solid white lines may also set general lanes apart from HOV lanes, or appear ahead of an obstruction you are allowed to pass on either side.

source_cards.front: What do double broken yellow lines side by side mark?
source_cards.back: Double broken yellow lines side by side mark the edges of a reversible lane, and you enter or leave that lane only as its signs and signals permit.

source_cards.front: How are the lines of a two-way left turn lane arranged?
source_cards.back: Solid-plus-broken yellow lines also outline a two-way left turn lane, with the solid lines on the outside and the broken lines on the inside.

source_cards.front: How do reversible-lane lines differ from two-way left turn lane lines?
source_cards.back: Double broken yellow lines outline a reversible lane, while solid outer lines with broken inner lines outline a two-way left turn lane.

source_cards.front: What do double solid yellow lines forbid?
source_cards.back: Double solid yellow lines divide opposing traffic and forbid passing from either direction.

source_cards.front: May you turn left across double solid yellow lines into a driveway?
source_cards.back: You are allowed to turn left across double solid yellow lines, for example to pull into a driveway.

source_cards.front: Where is a solid yellow line beside a broken yellow line used?
source_cards.back: A solid yellow line beside a broken yellow line is used on two-way roads where passing is allowed in only one direction.

source_cards.front: With a solid and a broken yellow line, what decides whether you may pass?
source_cards.back: With a solid line next to a broken yellow line, the rule depends on which line is nearer to you: broken on your side means you may pass with care, solid on your side means you may not.

source_cards.front: Double solid yellow bars passing. Does it also bar a left turn into a driveway?
source_cards.back: Double solid yellow lines bar passing, yet a left turn across them, such as into a driveway, is still allowed.

source_cards.front: How does a stop line differ from yield lines?
source_cards.back: A stop line is a single solid white line marking where to stop, while yield lines are rows of small triangles marking where to yield.

source_cards.front: Do most Maryland roads shared with bicycles have special bicycle markings?
source_cards.back: Most Maryland roads that bicycles share with motor vehicles carry no special signs or pavement markings for bicycles.

source_cards.front: Where are shared-use lane markings found mostly?
source_cards.back: Shared-use lane markings, found mostly in cities, warn drivers that cyclists may be present, show cyclists where to ride, and discourage riding against traffic.

source_cards.front: What separates bicycle-only lanes from motor vehicle lanes?
source_cards.back: Bicycle-only lanes are separated from motor vehicle lanes by solid or broken white lines and may be marked with bike lane signs or bicycle symbols and arrows.

source_cards.front: How do shared-use lane markings differ from a bike lane?
source_cards.back: Shared-use lane markings mean cyclists and drivers share a lane, whereas a bike lane is set apart for bicycles by solid or broken white lines.

needs.title: Skid and traction recovery

source_cards.front: Which of these reduces traction?
source_cards.back: Sand, gravel, rough pavement, oil, water and higher speed all reduce traction, which makes a skid or slide more likely.

source_cards.front: Without anti-lock brakes, how do you avoid skidding when braking?
source_cards.back: Slamming the brakes can start a skid; without an anti-lock braking system, pump the brakes to avoid skidding.

source_cards.front: In a skid, what should you do first with the pedal you are pressing?
source_cards.back: In a skid, first ease off whichever pedal you are pressing, gas or brake, to regain control.

source_cards.front: Which way should you steer in a skid?
source_cards.back: Steer in the direction of the skid and look where you want the vehicle to go.

source_cards.front: What happens when a vehicle hydroplanes?
source_cards.back: Hydroplaning happens when speed and standing water rise until the tires ride on a sheet of water and lose contact with the road, costing some or all control.

source_cards.front: How can you prevent hydroplaning?
source_cards.back: To prevent hydroplaning, keep tires in good shape and slow down on wet roads.

source_cards.front: If you start hydroplaning, what should you not do?
source_cards.back: If you start hydroplaning, lift off the gas, do not brake, keep the vehicle straight and slow until control returns.

source_cards.front: How does braking differ in a hydroplane versus a skid?
source_cards.back: In a hydroplane you do not brake, while in a skid you may brake once the tires grip again.

source_cards.front: How does Maryland law treat bicycles?
source_cards.back: Maryland law treats bicycles as vehicles; cyclists may use the road and must obey all traffic signals.

source_cards.front: Where should you not expect cyclists?
source_cards.back: Expect cyclists on every kind of road except interstates and tolled bridges and tunnels, at intersections and circles, in any weather and at any hour.

source_cards.front: With parked cars on the right, where is a cyclist often safest?
source_cards.back: Cyclists may ride in the travel lane for safety on narrow roads or to avoid hazards, and with no shoulder or with parked cars on the right the lane center is often safest.

source_cards.front: When may a Maryland cyclist take the full lane well below traffic speed?
source_cards.back: In Maryland a cyclist may take the full lane even well below traffic speed when the lane is too narrow for a vehicle to pass the bicycle safely within it.

source_cards.front: When you enter or cross a bike lane, whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Cyclists have the right-of-way when a motor vehicle turns, and you must yield to cyclists in a bike lane or shoulder you enter or cross.

source_cards.front: How do cyclists signal their turns?
source_cards.back: Cyclists use hand and arm signals since bicycles lack turn signals, and they may swerve or change speed suddenly to avoid holes or glass, so do not follow closely.

source_cards.front: How much room must you leave when passing a cyclist?
source_cards.back: Pass a cyclist as you would any slow vehicle, waiting for oncoming traffic to clear and leaving at least three feet, whether the bike is in a bike lane, on the shoulder or in your lane.

source_cards.front: After passing a cyclist, when do you move back into your lane?
source_cards.back: After passing a cyclist, see the bicycle in your rear-view mirror before moving back into your lane.

source_cards.front: Where a bridge narrows the road, what should you expect a shoulder cyclist to do?
source_cards.back: Where a bridge, parked cars or another obstruction narrows the road, expect a shoulder cyclist to merge left into the travel lane.

source_cards.front: At night, which headlights should you use as you approach a cyclist?
source_cards.back: At night a faint reflective object may be a bicycle in the travel lane, so use low beams as you approach a cyclist.

source_cards.front: Unless a cyclist signals a turn, what should you assume?
source_cards.back: Assume a cyclist is going straight through an intersection unless the rider signals a turn, and look both ways before crossing a sidewalk or trail.

source_cards.front: Before a right turn, what should you check for?
source_cards.back: Before a right turn, check your right side and blind spot for bikes and move as far right as you can within the bike lane, shoulder or right turn lane.

needs.title: Vehicle blind spots

source_cards.front: What are the large blind spots around trucks called?
source_cards.back: Trucks have four large blind spots, called no-zones, where other vehicles vanish from the driver's view.

source_cards.front: If you cannot see the truck driver's face in the side mirror, what does that mean?
source_cards.back: Side no-zones lie on both sides of trucks and buses; if you cannot see the driver's face in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

source_cards.front: How far does a truck's right-side blind spot reach?
source_cards.back: A truck's right-side blind spot runs the full length of the trailer and reaches out three lanes.

source_cards.front: Why should you not tailgate trucks and buses?
source_cards.back: Trucks and buses have huge rear no-zones, so do not tailgate them; the driver cannot see you and you have no escape if they stop suddenly.

source_cards.front: What is the rule for each truck no-zone?
source_cards.back: Each truck no-zone has its own rule: beside a truck, make sure you can see the driver's face in the mirror; behind it, do not tailgate; in front, do not cut in until both headlights show in your mirror.

source_cards.front: Why look twice before changing lanes?
source_cards.back: Look twice, using mirrors and a shoulder check, before merging or changing lanes, because a small motorcycle can hide in a blind spot.

source_cards.front: Before a right turn, what should you check for?
source_cards.back: Before a right turn, check your right side and blind spot for bikes and move as far right as you can within the bike lane, shoulder or right turn lane.

source_cards.front: Which of these is an example of a driver assistance system?
source_cards.back: Examples of ADAS are Automatic Emergency Braking, Lane Keeping Assistance and Blind Spot Warning, which use sensors and cameras to spot dangers.

source_cards.front: Where there is no signal, must you stop for a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk?

source_cards.front: Do most intersections have a crosswalk even without markings?
source_cards.back: A crosswalk is where pedestrians may cross and drivers must stop for them; some are painted, others are not, and most intersections have one even without markings.

source_cards.front: May you pass a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk?
source_cards.back: You may not pass any vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk.

source_cards.front: Why not stop beyond a stop line?
source_cards.back: Stopping beyond a stop line can put your vehicle in the path of trucks turning from the cross street.

source_cards.front: In a crosswalk, what right-of-way does a bicycle have?
source_cards.back: In a crosswalk a bicycle has the same right-of-way as a pedestrian, and failing to yield to a bicycle in a way that causes a crash brings fines and or prison time plus points.

source_cards.front: Who yields when a cyclist rides on a sidewalk?
source_cards.back: A turning driver must yield to cyclists, and in a crosswalk a cyclist gets the same right-of-way as a pedestrian, whereas a cyclist riding on a sidewalk must yield to pedestrians.

needs.title: Intersections and right-of-way

source_cards.front: Do pedestrians with the right-of-way still have to obey traffic signals?
source_cards.back: Pedestrians have the right-of-way at street crossings, but they too must obey traffic control signals.

source_cards.front: When do police cars, ambulances and fire engines have the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: Police cars, ambulances and fire engines have the right-of-way when their sirens and flashing lights are on.

source_cards.front: When you enter or cross a bike lane, whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Cyclists have the right-of-way when a motor vehicle turns, and you must yield to cyclists in a bike lane or shoulder you enter or cross.

source_cards.front: In a crosswalk, what right-of-way does a bicycle have?
source_cards.back: In a crosswalk a bicycle has the same right-of-way as a pedestrian, and failing to yield to a bicycle in a way that causes a crash brings fines and or prison time plus points.

source_cards.front: Who yields when a cyclist rides on a sidewalk?
source_cards.back: A turning driver must yield to cyclists, and in a crosswalk a cyclist gets the same right-of-way as a pedestrian, whereas a cyclist riding on a sidewalk must yield to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: Approaching a stopped tow truck, what should you do?
source_cards.back: Approaching a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck or other service vehicle, move to a lane not right next to it; if you cannot, slow to a safe speed and be ready to stop.

source_cards.front: A truck drifts left at an intersection. What should you do before passing on its right?
source_cards.back: Passing a truck on its right is risky, so wait to see whether a truck that drifts left is about to turn right before you pass.

source_cards.front: What danger comes from squeezing along a turning truck's right side?
source_cards.back: Never squeeze along the right side of a truck starting a turn at an intersection, or you may be trapped between it and the curb.

source_cards.front: When passing a same-direction truck, when may you return to its lane?
source_cards.back: Pass a same-direction truck quickly, and return to its lane only once both of its headlights show in your rear-view mirror.

source_cards.front: How far does a truck's right-side blind spot reach?
source_cards.back: A truck's right-side blind spot runs the full length of the trailer and reaches out three lanes.

source_cards.front: How much time and room do truck and bus drivers need to stop compared with cars?
source_cards.back: Truck and bus drivers need nearly twice the time and room that cars need to stop, so do not pull in front of them too soon after passing.

source_cards.front: How far must you stop from a school bus with flashing red lights when behind it?
source_cards.back: When a school bus stops with flashing red lights, stop at least twenty feet from its back if you are behind it, or twenty feet from its front if you are ahead of it.

needs.title: Motorcycle road position and visibility

source_cards.front: When turning left, whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Yield to an oncoming motorcycle when you turn left; failing to can bring a citation with significant penalties, and drivers are at fault in over half of car-motorcycle crashes.

source_cards.front: Why look twice before changing lanes?
source_cards.back: Look twice, using mirrors and a shoulder check, before merging or changing lanes, because a small motorcycle can hide in a blind spot.

source_cards.front: May you share a lane with a motorcycle?
source_cards.back: Never share a lane with a motorcycle; riders may use the whole lane and shift within it to avoid hazards, handle wind and be seen.

needs.title: Emergency vehicle approach and move-over

source_cards.front: What does Maryland's Move Over law require?
source_cards.back: Maryland's Move Over law requires you to move over when approaching any vehicle stopped, standing or parked on the road with its lights flashing.

source_cards.front: What is the basic Move Over penalty?
source_cards.back: Breaking the Move Over law is a misdemeanor carrying a one hundred ten dollars fine and one point on your license.

source_cards.front: What is the Move Over penalty when a violation causes a crash?
source_cards.back: A Move Over violation that causes a crash carries a one hundred fifty dollars fine and three points.

source_cards.front: What is the Move Over penalty when a death or serious injury results?
source_cards.back: A Move Over violation involving a death or serious injury carries a seven hundred fifty dollars fine and three points.

source_cards.front: How do Move Over penalties rise with harm?
source_cards.back: The basic Move Over penalty is one hundred ten dollars and one point, rising to one hundred fifty dollars and three points if a crash results and seven hundred fifty dollars and three points with a death or serious injury.
